prompt: New bags made deliveries 0.32 minutes faster, with p = 9 × 10⁻¹². What does the tiny p-value tell Horta?
hint: What does a p-value measure, and what does it not?

choices.text: That the bags make a large difference
choices.why: The p-value does not measure size; the difference is 0.32 minutes.

choices.text: That the difference is not chance
choices.why: Right. It is real, and it is still a third of a minute.

choices.text: That customers will notice the change
choices.why: Nineteen seconds is unlikely to be noticed.

choices.text: That the study was badly designed
choices.why: The design is fine; the sample is just very large.

prompt: A true difference of 0.3 minutes is tested with 50, then 5,000, then 100,000 deliveries per group. What happens to the p-value?
hint: What happens to the standard error?

choices.text: It stays about the same, like the effect
choices.why: The effect stays the same; the p-value does not.

choices.text: It grows, because more data adds noise
choices.why: More data shrinks the standard error.

choices.text: It cannot be computed for large samples
choices.why: It can; it just becomes extremely small.

choices.text: It shrinks towards zero as n grows
choices.why: Right. The standard error falls, so the same effect looks ever less like chance.

prompt: Two groups differ by 0.32 minutes, with a pooled standard deviation of 10.48. What is Cohen's d? Give two decimal places, as a positive number.
Two groups have means m1 and m2 and a pooled standard deviation s. Write Cohen's d.
A conversion rate rises from 11.0% to 13.1%. By what percentage of the old rate did it rise? Give the nearest whole number.
Why should a report give both the absolute and the relative change in a rate?
hint: How does 19% sound next to 2.1 points?

choices.text: Each alone distorts the size
choices.why: Right. Relative changes inflate small effects; absolute ones can shrink them.

choices.text: Because the relative change is always wrong
choices.why: It is correct arithmetic; it just needs the baseline beside it.

choices.text: Because tests need both to compute p
choices.why: A test needs the counts, not two ways of describing them.

choices.text: Because journals require two numbers
choices.why: The reason is the reader's understanding, not a rule.

prompt: When should the smallest effect worth acting on be chosen?
hint: Lesson 14's argument about deciding in advance.

choices.text: After the test, once the size is known
choices.why: A threshold chosen after the result drifts towards it.

choices.text: Never; the p-value decides
choices.why: The p-value cannot say what matters.

choices.text: Before the data, from costs and benefits
choices.why: Right. Then the result cannot bend it.

choices.text: Whenever the result is not significant
choices.why: It is needed for every result, and in advance.

prompt: The bags save about nineteen seconds per delivery, which no customer notices, and about 530 courier-hours a year. Do they matter?
hint: What is the effect multiplied by?

choices.text: No, since the effect size is tiny
choices.why: Tiny per delivery can be large in total; it depends on the question.

choices.text: Yes, since the result is significant
choices.why: Significance says it is real, not that it matters.

choices.text: It depends on what the new bags cost
choices.why: Right. The same effect is worth having at one price and not at another.

choices.text: No, because customers do not notice
choices.why: Couriers' time is worth something even if customers never see it.

prompt: Match each result to its place in the table of significant and important.
hint: Compare each interval with zero and with ±2 minutes.

prompt: The routing trial and the app trial were both not significant. Why do they mean opposite things?
hint: Look at where each interval ends.

choices.text: Only the app's interval stays inside ±2
choices.why: Right. The routing interval reaches effects that would matter; the app's does not.

choices.text: One used a one-sided test
choices.why: Sidedness does not explain it; the widths of the intervals do.

choices.text: The app's p-value was smaller
choices.why: The p-values do not settle what each trial rules out.

choices.text: The routing trial used fewer couriers
choices.why: Size matters through the interval width, which is the point.

prompt: The training course gave an interval of −2.4 to −0.03 minutes. With a threshold of 2 minutes, what is the honest conclusion?

choices.text: The course saves more than 2 minutes
choices.why: Most of the interval is below 2 minutes in size.

choices.text: The course does nothing
choices.why: The interval excludes zero.

choices.text: The course is too small to matter
choices.why: The interval reaches past 2 minutes, so it might matter.

choices.text: It helps, by an amount not yet clear
choices.why: Right. Probably real, possibly worth it, and a larger study would tell.

prompt: What does an equivalence test check?
hint: Too small to matter, shown positively.

choices.text: Whether two samples are the same size
choices.why: It is about the effect, not the samples.

choices.text: Whether the effect lies inside a band
choices.why: Right. Two one-sided tests, one against each edge.

choices.text: Whether the effect is exactly zero
choices.why: That is what an ordinary test asks, and it can never confirm it.

choices.text: Whether the p-value is below 0.05
choices.why: That is the ordinary rule, not the equivalence question.

prompt: A 50-delivery trial of the bags gave p = 0.45 and an interval of −5.18 to +2.29 minutes. What may Horta conclude?
hint: What does the interval leave open?

choices.text: The bags have no effect
choices.why: The interval allows anything from five minutes saved to two lost.

choices.text: Too little data to tell
choices.why: Right. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

choices.text: The bags slow deliveries by 2.29 minutes
choices.why: That is just the upper end of a wide interval.

choices.text: The 100,000-delivery result was wrong
choices.why: The small trial is consistent with it; it is just far less precise.

prompt: Why do small studies that do reach significance tend to exaggerate the effect?

choices.text: Small samples have larger true effects
choices.why: The true effect does not depend on the sample.

choices.text: Their p-values are computed wrongly
choices.why: The arithmetic is fine; the selection is the problem.

choices.text: Researchers round their results up
choices.why: No dishonesty is needed for this to happen.

choices.text: Only the lucky samples cross the line
choices.why: Right. The winner's curse of lesson 15.

prompt: Put these steps of an analysis in the order the checklist gives them.
hint: Before the data, with the data, in the report.
items: Decide the smallest effect that would matter
Look at the data before summarising it
Report the estimate with its interval

prompt: Which belong in an honest report of a test? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The estimate and its confidence interval
choices.why: Yes: size and uncertainty first.

choices.text: The exact p-value
choices.why: Yes: not just "p < 0.05".

choices.text: "Significant" in place of the size
choices.why: The word says nothing about how big the effect is.

choices.text: How many tests were run
choices.why: Yes: one of twenty is a different finding.

prompt: Cohen's d, a difference measured in standard deviations, is one kind of ___ ___.
A saving of 0.32 minutes per delivery across 100,000 deliveries a year is how many hours? Give the nearest whole number.
